title: Forming passive sentences 1
subtitle: We were given that vase.
summary: Work out which passive forms a verb allows - two objects, object + complement, object + bare infinitive, or a multi-word verb.

lesson.heading: Verbs with two objects
lesson.text: Verbs such as *give* take both a direct object (DO) and an indirect object (IO), in two patterns: **verb + IO + DO** or **verb + DO + preposition + IO**. These verbs therefore have **two** corresponding passives, and you choose whichever suits the context. If you name the agent, it follows **by** at the end of the clause.

examples.text: Alice gave us that vase. - **We were given** that vase (by Alice).
Alice gave that vase to us. - **That vase was given (to) us** (by Alice).
examples.note: in informal contexts to can be left out

lesson.note: Also: award, hand, lend, offer, send, throw ('giving' verbs); ask, read, teach ('telling' verbs).

lesson.heading: Active to passive
rows: Alice gave us that vase. (V + IO + DO)
We were given that vase (by Alice).
Alice gave that vase to us. (V + DO + to + IO)
That vase was given (to) us (by Alice).
He explained the problem to me. (no IO + DO pattern)
The problem was explained to me.

lesson.heading: Verbs with only one passive
lesson.text: Verbs that cannot be followed by IO + DO in the active have only **one** passive: the direct object becomes the subject and the person follows a preposition.

examples.text: He explained the problem to me. - **The problem was explained to me.**
Improvements **have been proposed** to the developers.

lesson.note: Also: announce, demonstrate, describe, introduce, mention, propose, report, suggest ('reporting' verbs).

lesson.heading: Object + complement
lesson.text: Verbs followed by object + complement in the active have one passive form: the object becomes the subject and the complement stays where it is.

examples.text: They elected her president. - **She was elected president.**
Alan Watson **was declared** winner of the election after a recount.

lesson.note: Also: appoint, declare, make, nominate, vote (giving someone a position); call, name, title ('naming' verbs).

lesson.heading: A bare infinitive becomes a to-infinitive
lesson.text: Some verbs followed by object + **bare infinitive** (an infinitive without *to*) in the active are followed by a **to-infinitive** in the passive.

examples.text: They have made him return the money. - He has been made **to** return the money.
People helped Rob to his feet. - Rob **was helped** to his feet.

lesson.note: Also: feel, hear, help (also + object + to-infinitive), observe, see.

lesson.heading: Two- and three-word verbs
lesson.text: Some transitive multi-word verbs have passive forms, but others are never used in the passive.

examples.text: Ella looked after him. - He **was looked after** (by Ella).
examples.note: also carry out, disapprove of, hold over, talk down to

examples.text: We came up against a problem.
examples.wrong: A problem was come up against
examples.note: also brush up on, cast (your mind) back, get (something) down, take after

lesson.heading: One verb, one sense passive
lesson.text: Some multi-word verbs are only used in the passive with **certain senses** of the verb.

examples.text: They put out the fire. - **The fire was put out.**
I put out a hand to steady myself.
examples.wrong: A hand was put out to steady myself

lesson.note: Passive possible / no passive: call (someone) up (order to join the army / telephone); call (someone) back (ask to return / telephone); let in (allow into a place / allow rain in); let out (allow to leave / let out a sound).

lesson.text: Before you write a passive, check the active pattern: only a verb that can say gave us that vase can also say we were given that vase.

exercises.prompt: Someone handed me a note. - ___ a note.
exercises.explanation: hand is a 'giving' verb, so the indirect object can become the subject.

exercises.prompt: Someone awarded him a prize. - ___ a prize.
exercises.explanation: Two passives are possible: He was awarded a prize. / A prize was awarded to him.

exercises.prompt: Someone has lent me some skis. - ___ some skis.
exercises.explanation: Keep the tense of the active: has lent becomes have been lent.

exercises.statement: I was explained the problem by my tutor.
exercises.explanation: The problem was explained to me by my tutor. explain cannot be followed by an indirect object + direct object, so it has only one passive.

exercises.prompt: Someone is sending me a lot of spam emails. - ___ a lot of spam emails.
exercises.explanation: The present continuous passive is am/is/are being + past participle.

exercises.prompt: Someone is going to explain the changes to the students. Which passive is right?
options: The changes are going to be explained to the students.
The students are going to be explained the changes.
The changes are going to explain to the students.
exercises.explanation: explain has only one passive: the direct object becomes the subject and the person follows to.

exercises.prompt: Someone had mentioned the password to the thieves. - The password ___ to the thieves.
exercises.explanation: mention is a 'reporting' verb: only The password had been mentioned to the thieves is possible.

exercises.prompt: Make a passive sentence: they appointed Sven Larsen to the Scandinavian job last week.
exercises.answer: Sven Larsen has been appointed Regional Sales Director for Scandinavia
exercises.explanation: After appoint the complement (Regional Sales Director) stays in place in the passive.

exercises.prompt: They have made him return the money. - He has ___ the money.
exercises.explanation: A bare infinitive after make becomes a to-infinitive in the passive.

exercises.statement: Strict teachers are often looked up to by children.
exercises.explanation: Correct. look up to is one of the multi-word verbs that does have a passive form.

exercises.prompt: Which of these verbs can be used in the passive, and which cannot?

items.text: hold over (an item until the next meeting)

exercises.prompt: The farmer prevented walkers from crossing the field after he fenced it off. - Walkers were prevented from crossing the field after ___ (by the farmer).
exercises.explanation: fence off has a passive form, so both clauses can be made passive.
